Tiny golden pearls, deep-fried until crisp, are dropped into whisked curd where they plump up and soften at the edges while staying faintly chewy in the centre.
A wedding-buffet favourite across North India, it lands somewhere between crunchy and squishy in every spoonful, dusted with roasted cumin and red chilli.
A gram-flour-pearl version of India's whisked-curd side, its tiny fried nuggets soaking up tang as they sit.
fact: The tiny fried droplets are made by pushing gram-flour batter through a perforated ladle straight into hot oil — the same technique used to make the sweet dessert version of the same droplet.

name: Mint Chutney
clues: A bright, herb-forward blend that needs no flame — everything goes raw into the grinder.
Built on a cooling green herb prized for its menthol bite, balanced with tart citrus and a raw green chilli or two.
Ladled onto grilled skewers and stuffed snacks alike, its sharp, palate-cleansing edge cuts through fried and smoky flavours.
India's herb-based dip, also called pudina after the Hindi word for the leaf that gives it its cooling punch.
fact: This chutney oxidizes and turns brown within hours of blending, which is why street vendors grind it fresh in small batches throughout the day instead of making it ahead.

name: Tamarind Chutney
clues: A sweet-and-sour cooked syrup that takes its tang from a sticky brown pod pulp, simmered down slowly on the stove.
Jaggery and dried ginger get simmered into the sour pulp until it turns thick, dark, and pourable, almost like a fruit syrup.
An essential drizzle over crisp street snacks and stuffed pastries, adding sweetness where other dips only bring heat.
The sweet-sour imli version, made from the pulp of a tangy pod, that finishes so many roadside chaat plates.
fact: It's one of the two essential sauces — the other being a green herb blend — that give pani puri and other chaats their signature sweet-sour-spicy balance.

name: Coconut Chutney
clues: A South Indian staple ground fresh each morning, pale white and flecked with green, served in a small steel bowl beside breakfast.
Made from the grated white flesh of a hard-shelled tropical fruit, its milk-rich sweetness is cut with raw green chilli and roasted lentils.
A final tempering of mustard seeds and curry leaves crackled in hot oil is poured over just before it reaches the table.
The coconut-based dip that rounds out a plate of dosa or idli, all creamy sweetness against the batter's tang.
fact: In much of Tamil Nadu and Kerala it's ground fresh at nearly every meal, since the grated flesh it's built from turns rancid within a day without refrigeration.

name: Tomato Chutney
clues: A cooked-down side with a deep red colour and a savoury-sweet tang, simmered slowly rather than ground raw.
A juicy, acidic salad fruit — technically a berry — is stewed with onion, garlic, and dried red chillies until it collapses into a jammy paste.
Popular in South Indian households as a spicier, tangier alternative to the classic coconut-based dip, it pairs beautifully with crisp lentil crepes.
A stewed red-fruit version of South India's tangy tempered side, cooked down until sweet, sour, and deeply coloured.
fact: It's often finished with a spoonful of jaggery to round out the fruit's acidity, and goes by thakkali chutney in Tamil kitchens.

name: Peanut Chutney
clues: A South Indian favourite made almost entirely from a single roasted legume, ground with dried chillies into something thick and reddish-brown.
The seeds are dry-roasted in a hot pan until their skins loosen and their aroma turns nutty, then blitzed with garlic and a whisper of sour pulp.
Coarser and heartier than most South Indian dips, it holds its texture rather than turning silky smooth, and pairs especially well with steamed rice cakes.
The groundnut version of South India's tempered dip, its roasted, earthy crunch a contrast to the cooling coconut kind.
fact: It's a specialty of Andhra Pradesh, where cooks often reach for it over the coconut version when coconuts are scarce or expensive.

name: Mango Pickle
clues: A preserved condiment that takes weeks, not minutes — jars of it sit in the sun to mature before they're ready to eat.
Made from a hard, sour stone fruit picked while still green and unripe, chopped into rough pieces and layered with pungent seed spices.
Mustard oil, fenugreek, and a generous hand of chilli powder coat every piece, turning fiercely sour and hot as it cures.
The classic green aam achar of Indian households, a jar of sun-cured stone fruit that outlasts entire monsoon seasons in the pantry.
fact: A well-cured batch is traditionally left to mature in a sun-warmed glass or ceramic jar for at least a week, with the mustard oil deepening in colour as it soaks up the chilli and spices.

name: Mixed Pickle
clues: A preserved jar condiment that isn't built around one single ingredient but a whole medley of chopped vegetables curing together.
Cauliflower florets, carrot batons, turnip cubes, and slivers of green chilli all share the same pungent mustard-oil bath.
Each vegetable keeps a bit of its own crunch and colour even after weeks of curing, so no two spoonfuls look quite alike.
India's assorted vegetable achar, a jumble of textures preserved together in one fiery, oil-slicked jar.
fact: Because it combines vegetables with very different densities and moisture levels, some households still finish it with a few days of direct sun exposure to draw out excess water before sealing the jar.

name: Roasted Papad
clues: A paper-thin lentil wafer that puffs and blisters when it meets direct heat, with no oil involved at all.
Held over an open flame or a bare gas burner with tongs, it crackles, curls, and darkens with faint char spots in seconds.
Its smoky, slightly bitter edge comes purely from fire, unlike its deep-fried cousin which stays pale and glassy.
The flame-roasted disc known across India as papadum, snapped into shards alongside a thali.
fact: Holding it over the flame is considered a small kitchen skill in itself: held too close it scorches in seconds, held too far it never blisters properly.

name: Masala Papad
clues: A crisp lentil-wafer base gets dressed up like a mini open-faced salad just before it's served, never allowed to sit long.
Finely chopped onion, tomato, and green chilli are scattered over the fried or flame-cooked disc, with a squeeze of lemon and a dusting of tangy spice blend.
It must be eaten within moments of assembly, or the topping's moisture turns the crackly base soft and limp.
The loaded, chaat-style version of India's lentil wafer, its spiced topping turning a plain snack into a five-minute street food.
fact: It became a fixture on Indian restaurant menus as an instant starter precisely because it needs no real cooking beyond crisping the base, so kitchens can plate it almost immediately.

name: Chicken Tikka Masala
clues: Born not in a kitchen but a debate — food historians still argue whether this creamy chicken dish is a British invention or a genuine subcontinental creation.
Legend credits a curry house chef in Glasgow with rescuing a customer's dry send-back by drowning it in a tomato-cream sauce.
Chunks of chicken, marinated and cooked in a tandoor, are folded into a rich tomato-cream gravy.
Often called Britain's national dish, this chicken curry pairs char-grilled, marinated chicken pieces with a velvety tomato-cream sauce.
fact: A 2001 UK parliamentary motion half-jokingly declared Chicken Tikka Masala 'a true British national dish,' fueling the origin debate further.

name: Kadai Chicken
clues: Named after the thick, wide wok-like pan it's tossed in over high flame, not after any spice or region.
Coarsely pounded coriander seeds and dried red chillies give this dish its rustic, flecked masala rather than a smooth puree.
Bell peppers and onions are cut into chunky diamonds and stir-fried fast at high heat, keeping the dish semi-dry rather than swimming in gravy.
Known in many kitchens as karahi chicken, this dry, chunky curry is finished with julienned ginger and green chillies for a sharp bite.
fact: Kadai Chicken is traditionally finished by drizzling melted butter or ghee over the top just before it leaves the pan.

name: Chicken Chettinad
clues: Hails from a merchant community in Tamil Nadu famed for pounding a fiery, fragrant spice blend fresh for every pot rather than using a pre-mixed powder.
A curious lichen called kalpasi, or stone flower, is one of the secret ingredients that gives this curry its distinctive earthy aroma.
Star anise, fennel seeds, and a fistful of dried red chillies are dry-roasted and ground into a dark, intensely peppery masala for this South Indian chicken curry.
This peppery, dark chicken curry, named for a spice-trading region of Tamil Nadu famed for its pepper and stone-flower blends, is one of South India's most fiery classics.
fact: Chicken Chettinad can use up to fifteen or twenty different spices, freshly ground for each batch rather than stored as a masala powder.

name: Chicken 65
clues: A late-night bar snack from Chennai, its numerical name has spawned more origin myths than almost any other Indian dish.
Some say it began as an item on a hotel menu numbered by year, others claim it needed exactly that many chillies or that many days to marinate — no one agrees.
Bite-sized pieces of deboned chicken are deep-fried until fiery red and crisp, then flash-tossed with curry leaves, green chillies, and a tempering of mustard seeds.
Reputedly invented at Chennai's Buhari Hotel, this deep-red, deep-fried chicken starter carries a numeric name whose origin nobody can agree on — some insist it's simply the year 1965.
fact: Chicken 65's name is so contested that even the Buhari Hotel, its reputed birthplace, has offered multiple conflicting explanations over the years.

name: Chicken Korma
clues: A Mughlai classic where the meat is braised gently in its own steam with yogurt and ground nuts, never touched by tomato.
Cashews, almonds, or melon seeds are ground into a paste to thicken this pale, fragrant gravy instead of a chilli-forward masala.
Famous for its restraint — whole spices like cardamom and mace perfume the dish rather than making it fiery, and the colour stays ivory to golden.
This mild, creamy braise, sometimes spelled with a q or a k, is a Mughal-court legacy prized for its nutty richness rather than heat.
fact: Chicken Korma traces back to the Mughal kitchens of the sixteenth century, where restraint with chilli was considered refined, not bland.

name: Andhra Chicken Curry
clues: Comes from a coastal state whose chillies are so notoriously potent they're a major chilli-export hub of India.
Sesame oil and a heavy hand with garlic and red chilli powder define this fiery curry, often cooked in a clay pot for extra smokiness.
In its home region, this dish is called by a local word for chicken paired with a local word for curry — a fiercely spiced, thin, gravy-forward preparation quite unlike its creamier northern cousins.
Known locally as kodi kura, this blisteringly hot curry from a southeastern coastal state leans on dried red chillies and curry leaves for its punch.
fact: Andhra Chicken Curry often uses Guntur chillies, grown in a district that supplies a huge share of India's chilli exports.

name: Laal Maas
clues: A Rajput hunters' dish from the desert state of Rajasthan, traditionally made with wild game before mutton became the norm.
Its blazing colour comes from a specific variety of dried red chilli grown near Jodhpur, used in eye-watering quantity.
Yogurt tempers the heat of this thick, fiery mutton curry, which was historically cooked over open fires during royal hunting expeditions.
Literally translating to 'red meat' in Rajasthani, this fiery mutton curry gets its name from its chilli-soaked colour.
fact: Laal Maas was traditionally a dish for Rajput warriors returning from a hunt, cooked with whatever game they'd brought back that day.

name: Mutton Korma
clues: This slow-braised, richly spiced curry relies on a base of browned onions and yogurt rather than tomatoes for its body.
Whole warming spices — cinnamon, cardamom, cloves — steep into the gravy while the meat turns fall-apart tender over a long, low simmer.
A nut and onion paste thickens this mellow, aromatic goat-meat preparation, keeping the heat gentle even though the meat itself is robust and gamey.
Often labelled with a q instead of a k, this rich, slow-braised goat-meat dish shares its yogurt-and-nut base with a beloved chicken cousin.
fact: Mutton Korma is a centerpiece of Eid and wedding feasts across North India, often simmered for hours the day before serving.

name: Mutton Sukka
clues: A coastal Karnataka specialty where the meat is cooked down until almost no liquid remains, clinging instead to a dark, roasted coconut coating.
Freshly grated coconut is dry-roasted until deeply browned before being ground into the masala, giving this preparation its smoky, nutty crust.
Black pepper rather than red chilli often supplies the heat in this bone-in goat-meat dish, finished almost gravy-free and intensely aromatic.
This bone-in goat-meat preparation, whose name simply means 'dry' in regional Konkani and Tulu kitchens, is roasted with coconut until nearly no sauce is left.
fact: Mutton Sukka is a signature of Mangalorean and Konkani coastal cooking, where coconut is roasted rather than used raw as in most other curries.

name: Keema Matar
clues: A humble, home-style curry built from minced meat rather than chunks, simmered until it clings to a thick tomato-onion masala.
Green peas are folded in toward the end, adding a pop of sweetness and colour to this otherwise deep-brown, spice-heavy skillet dish.
Because the meat is ground fine, this dish cooks fast and is a weeknight staple often paired with flatbread or pav rather than rice.
This minced-meat-and-pea skillet dish, its two-word name literally naming its main components, is North Indian comfort food at its simplest.
fact: Keema Matar is one of the few Indian curries commonly eaten stuffed inside a bread roll, as in Mumbai's keema pav.

name: Pork Vindaloo
clues: Descended from a Portuguese sailors' dish of meat preserved in wine and garlic, adapted in Goa with local vinegar and chillies.
Its fiery reputation on British curry-house menus overshadows the fact that the original coastal version contains no root vegetable at all.
Vinegar does double duty here — as a tenderizer marinating the meat overnight and as the tang that cuts through the heat of the final braise.
Named after a mangled Portuguese phrase for garlic and wine, this vinegar-spiked, chilli-hot Goan pork classic is often wrongly assumed to always include potatoes.
fact: Pork Vindaloo's ancestor, carne de vinha d'alhos, was a Portuguese method of preserving meat with wine and garlic during long sea voyages.

name: Goan Fish Curry
clues: A coastal curry whose souring agent is often a dried mangosteen-relative fruit called kokum rather than tamarind or lime.
Ground coconut and a paste of dried red chillies form the base of this curry, traditionally eaten daily with plain steamed rice.
Mustard seeds and curry leaves crackle in hot oil as the final tempering poured over this tangy, coconut-rich curry from India's smallest state.
Sometimes called by its Konkani name meaning 'rice curry,' this everyday coconut-and-kokum curry is the backbone of India's western coastal table.
fact: Goan Fish Curry is eaten almost daily in Goan households, with the exact recipe varying noticeably between Hindu and Catholic kitchens.

name: Meen Moilee
clues: A gently spiced coastal curry from Kerala where coconut milk is added at the very end and never boiled hard, to keep it silky rather than split.
Turmeric and green chillies do the flavouring here instead of a heavy red chilli powder, giving this curry a pale golden hue.
Associated with Kerala's Syrian Christian community, this mild curry is a favourite at Sunday lunches and festive spreads alike.
Known regionally as fish molee, this delicately coconut-milk-based curry from India's southwest coast trades heat for gentle, aromatic sweetness.
fact: Meen Moilee is especially popular among Kerala's Syrian Christian community and is a fixture at their festive Onam and Christmas tables.

name: Fish Tikka Masala
clues: A newer spin-off of a wildly popular British curry-house creation, swapping the usual poultry for firm fillets instead.
Cubes of fish are first char-marinated in yogurt and spices before being folded into a rich tomato-cream gravy, so they hold their shape rather than flaking apart.
Because delicate flesh cooks fast and breaks easily, chefs sear it hard first, then add it to the sauce right at the end rather than simmering it in from the start.
This dish takes the beloved tomato-cream tandoori chicken curry template and reimagines it with fish, chunk for chunk.
fact: Fish Tikka Masala is a relatively recent addition to Indian restaurant menus abroad, riding on the coattails of its chicken predecessor's fame.

name: Prawn Balchao
clues: A Goan preserve-style curry so heavily laced with vinegar and chilli that it was designed to keep for weeks without refrigeration.
Sailors and traders once carried preparations like this one on long voyages, since the acidity acted as a natural preservative for the seafood inside.
A small amount of jaggery balances the fierce vinegar tang in this thick, deep-red, intensely piquant Goan seafood pickle-curry.
This tangy, fiery Goan shellfish pickle-curry, whose Portuguese-derived name refers to a spiced vinegar preserve, is eaten sparingly as a condiment rather than a main course.
fact: Prawn Balchao can be stored for weeks without refrigeration thanks to its heavy vinegar content, a trick inherited from Goa's Portuguese past.

name: Chingri Malai Curry
clues: A festive Bengali curry that looks rich enough for cream but actually gets its silky body from coconut milk, not dairy.
Jumbo river shellfish, prized and pricier than the small kind, are the traditional choice for this celebratory coastal Bengali curry.
Bay leaf, cardamom, and a touch of sugar give this mild, fragrant curry a delicate sweetness unusual among Bengali seafood preparations.
This Bengali wedding-feast shellfish curry gets its silky richness from coconut milk, not the dairy cream its English nickname might suggest.
fact: Chingri Malai Curry is a fixture of Bengali wedding feasts, traditionally made with the prized golda chingri, or giant river prawn.

name: Egg Curry
clues: One of the most common vegetarian-adjacent proteins gets simmered whole or halved in a spiced onion-tomato gravy in kitchens across the country.
Often the fallback dish for busy weeknights, since its main protein needs only boiling before it goes into the pot.
Shallow slits or halves are cut into the boiled protein before it's added, letting the gravy's spices seep all the way through.
This everyday onion-tomato gravy, built around boiled eggs rather than meat, is sometimes called anda curry using the Hindi word for its star ingredient.
fact: Egg Curry is one of India's most improvised dishes — nearly every region and household has its own version of the recipe.

name: Kosha Mangsho
clues: A Bengali Sunday ritual dish, traditionally simmered for hours in mustard oil until the gravy turns almost black and clings thickly to the meat.
Mountains of sliced onions are browned down slowly to form the base of this dark, intensely reduced mutton preparation.
The meat is marinated overnight in yogurt and mustard oil, then fried down hard before any water is added, concentrating the flavour into a thick coating rather than a thin gravy.
This deeply reduced, near-black Bengali mutton preparation, its name literally describing the slow-frying technique used on the meat, is a beloved Sunday lunch classic.
fact: Kosha Mangsho is a beloved Sunday lunch tradition in Bengali households, often paired with luchi, a puffed fried bread, rather than rice.

name: Lucknowi Mutton Biryani
clues: Nawabi kitchens favored a gentler hand with chile and a heavier one with whole spice and rosewater, producing a fragrant meat-and-rice dish milder than its Deccani cousin.
Here the meat is cooked to tenderness in its own korma-style gravy before ever meeting the rice, a two-pot method different from the raw-marinated approach used further south.
Threads of saffron and a splash of kewra water perfume layers that are sealed and finished over low coals rather than a fierce flame.
The nawabi city on the Gomti lent its refined court style to this milder, pakki-layered rice-and-meat classic, finished with rose and saffron perfume.
fact: Lucknowi biryani follows the pakki method, in which the mutton is cooked in its own korma-style gravy before being layered with parboiled rice, giving it a softer, more melded flavor than Hyderabad's raw-marinated kacchi style.

name: Kolkata Biryani
clues: Legend says a deposed king arrived here with his cooks but not his fortune, and one humble tuber was added to stretch the meat further.
A whole boiled potato, golden and soft, sits nestled among the meat pieces — as essential to fans of this eastern rendition as the meat itself.
Sweetened lightly with a touch of sugar and perfumed with kewra rather than heavy chile, it favors fragrance over fire.
The Bengal capital's rendition of the sealed rice-and-meat classic is famous above all for the whole potato hidden in every serving.
fact: Kolkata's version traces to the exiled Nawab Wajid Ali Shah of Awadh, whose limited budget for meat in 1856 Calcutta led his cooks to bulk up the dish with whole potatoes and eggs — a twist that became the dish's signature.

name: Veg Dum Biryani
clues: The meatless version of the sealed-pot classic relies on paneer or soy chunks and a colorful mix of produce to fill in for meat entirely.
Layers of saffron rice rest over a spiced mix of produce and paneer, and the pot is closed tight so trapped steam does the final cooking.
Popular at weddings and festive vegetarian spreads, it proves the celebrated layering technique never truly needed meat to shine.
A fully plant-based, paneer-and-vegetable take on the layered, steam-sealed rice classic served at festive occasions.
fact: Veg Dum Biryani proves the celebrated dum layering technique works just as well without meat, using paneer, soy chunks, or extra vegetables to soak up the saffron and whole-spice perfume.

name: Jeera Rice
clues: Whole aromatic seeds are bloomed in hot ghee until they crackle, then folded through fluffy long-grain rice with barely another spice in sight.
It's the everyday partner spooned alongside a bowl of creamy black lentils in North Indian home kitchens and restaurants alike.
Its whole flavor comes from just one toasted spice, letting the seeds' warm, earthy aroma carry the entire plate.
A simple North Indian side of basmati tempered only with toasted cumin seeds and ghee.
fact: Jeera rice pairs so often with dal makhani in North Indian restaurants that many menus list the two exclusively as a set combo.

name: Ghee Rice
clues: Clarified butter, cooked slowly until nutty, is the entire soul of this fragrant Malabar accompaniment.
Whole cinnamon, cloves and cardamom simmer into the fat before the rice ever goes in, along with cashews and raisins fried to a golden crisp.
A cherished side at Kerala Muslim wedding feasts, it's traditionally paired with a spicy meat or egg curry called salna.
The Malabar coast's rich, mildly sweet basmati side, cooked in browned clarified butter with whole spices, nuts and raisins.
fact: Known as neychoru in Malayalam, Kerala's ghee rice is a fixture of Malabar Muslim wedding feasts, always served alongside a spicy meat or egg curry called salna.

name: Peas Pulao
clues: A humble, mildly spiced rice dish studded with tender little orbs that are secretly a legume, cooked together so the rice drinks in their sweetness.
Whole spices like bay leaf and clove scent the pot, but the real star is a vegetable that's actually a legume in disguise.
A lunchbox and tiffin staple across North India, often the simplest dish on a wedding buffet table.
A simple basmati pilaf built around sweet green legume seeds and whole warm spices.
fact: Peas pulao is a fixture of North Indian tiffins and wedding buffets, prized for how the sweetness of green peas balances the whole warm spices.

name: Kashmiri Pulao
clues: Fruit and nuts, not chile, define this festive rice dish — apple, pineapple, pomegranate seeds and dried fruit tumble through the grains.
Milk and saffron lend it a pale golden hue and a delicate sweetness closer to dessert than dinner.
Named for a mountain valley famed for its orchards and saffron fields, it turns fruit into the main event on the plate.
A fruit-and-nut studded, saffron-scented sweet basmati dish from the Himalayan valley renowned for saffron.
fact: Kashmiri pulao often appears as the sweet finale of a Wazwan feast, its fruit and nuts standing in where other pulaos would use meat.

name: Lemon Rice
clues: A South Indian tempered rice dish gets its bright yellow color from turmeric and its tang from a common kitchen citrus fruit.
Mustard seeds, curry leaves, peanuts and chana dal crackle in hot oil before the cooked rice is tossed through with citrus juice.
A temple-prasadam favorite in Karnataka, it travels well in tiffin boxes since the acid keeps it fresh for hours.
A bright citrus-soured, turmeric-yellow tempered rice from South India, crunchy with peanuts and curry leaves.
fact: Lemon rice is offered as prasadam in many South Indian temples, particularly during festivals like Ugadi, prized for staying fresh without refrigeration thanks to its acidity.

name: Tamarind Rice
clues: A South Indian tempered rice dish built on a sour fruit-pulp paste that also flavors many chutneys and sambars.
Sesame oil, red chilies, fenugreek and roasted lentils go into a thick tangy paste that's mixed through cooled rice, often days after cooking without spoiling.
A festival and travel-friendly favorite in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, sometimes sold ready-made as a spice-paste mix in jars.
A deeply tangy, sesame-oil-rich tempered rice soured with a dark fruit pulp paste, a South Indian travel classic.
fact: Tamarind rice is central to Karnataka's Gowri and Ganesha festival offerings, and its tangy sesame-oil masala is sold ready-made in jars across South India as a shortcut mix.

name: Curd Rice
clues: The coolest dish on a South Indian thali, this one is finished raw and chilled rather than cooked further.
Cooked rice is mashed soft and mixed with fermented milk, then tempered with mustard seeds, curry leaves and sometimes pomegranate or grape.
Served last at traditional meals to soothe the stomach after spicy courses, it's also offered to deities in some South Indian temples.
A cooling, fermented-dairy-mixed rice from South India, served as the final course to calm the palate.
fact: Curd rice traditionally closes a South Indian meal because its cooling, probiotic-rich yogurt is believed to soothe the stomach after spicy courses.

name: Tomato Rice
clues: A one-pot South Indian rice dish where a common red salad fruit is cooked down into a tangy, glossy base before the rice goes in.
Onion, green chile and whole spices are sautéed until the sauce thickens, then rice is folded in until every grain turns a soft orange-red.
A quick tiffin-box classic in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu kitchens, often dressed up with a dollop of ghee or a fried egg on top.
A tangy, orange-red South Indian rice dish built on a thick simmered red-fruit base.
fact: Tomato rice is a quick lunchbox staple across Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, often finished with a fried egg or a dollop of ghee for richness.

name: Coconut Rice
clues: A South Indian temple-offering rice dish leans on a tropical fruit's grated white flesh for its richness rather than any dairy.
Mustard seeds, urad dal, cashews and curry leaves are fried in oil, then tossed with rice and freshly grated coconut for a delicate sweetness.
Common as prasadam in temples across Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, it's often garnished with fried cashews and raisins.
A South Indian rice dish enriched with freshly grated coconut and a crunchy tempering of lentils and cashews.
fact: Coconut rice is a common temple prasadam across Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, its natural sweetness needing no added sugar.

name: Moong Dal Khichdi
clues: A one-pot rice-and-split-lentil porridge often called India's ultimate comfort food, gentle enough for infants, invalids and elders alike.
Golden split lentils and rice cook down together with turmeric and cumin until soft and almost soupy, finished with a pool of melted ghee.
Ayurveda praises it as the easiest dish to digest, and it's traditionally the first solid food given to babies.
A soft, one-pot rice-and-lentil porridge, India's classic soothing comfort food.
fact: Khichdi is so deeply woven into Indian identity that in 2017 the government floated it as a candidate for the country's national dish.

name: Ven Pongal
clues: A South Indian breakfast porridge blends rice and yellow split lentils into a soft, savory mash rich with cracked pepper and cumin.
Ghee-fried cashews and curry leaves crown a dish traditionally cooked in a mud pot as an offering during the harvest festival season.
Served hot with coconut chutney and a tangy lentil stew, it's a temple and tiffin-counter breakfast staple in Tamil Nadu.
A savory, pepper-and-cumin spiced rice-and-lentil breakfast mash from Tamil Nadu, garnished with ghee-fried cashews.
fact: Ven pongal is traditionally cooked in a clay pot during the Tamil harvest festival of Pongal, where the pot is allowed to boil over as a symbol of abundance.

name: Vangi Bath
clues: This Karnataka one-pot rice dish leans on a purple-skinned nightshade vegetable and a special roasted spice blend ground fresh for it.
Coriander seeds, dried red chilies, chana dal and sesame are dry-roasted and ground into a fragrant powder unique to this dish, then cooked with rice and chunks of the vegetable.
A festival lunch-box favorite across Karnataka, distinct from the tamarind-based rice mixes because of its own dedicated spice masala.
A Karnataka rice dish built on chunks of purple brinjal and a dry-roasted spice powder made just for it.
fact: Vangi bath gets its distinct flavor from a dedicated spice blend called Vangi Bath powder, dry-roasted from coriander, chana dal, sesame and red chilies specifically for this dish.

name: Bagara Rice
clues: A Hyderabadi tempered rice dish gets its nutty crunch from roasted peanuts and sesame seeds folded through whole-spice-scented grains.
Curry leaves, cinnamon, cloves and bay leaf perfume the oil before rice ever touches the pot, yet there's no heavy sauce mixed in — just a light tempering.
A daily-table companion in Hyderabadi Muslim homes, often paired with a tangy sour lentil stew or a peanut-and-sesame vegetable curry.
A subtly spiced, peanut-and-sesame tempered basmati side from Hyderabad's home kitchens, distinct from its more famous layered cousin.
fact: Bagara rice is Hyderabad's everyday counterpart to biryani — a lightly spiced, nutty tempered rice usually paired with tangy dishes like mirchi ka salan or khatti dal.
